# Differentiating Clinical Pathogenicity from Asymptomatic Colonization in Diarrhoeagenic *Escherichia coli*: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical Meta-Analysis

### Abstract

#### Background

Diarrhoeagenic *Escherichia coli* (DEC) remains a primary bacterial cause of childhood morbidity, growth faltering, and mortality in Africa and globally. However, molecular surveillance studies frequently report DEC prevalence in asymptomatic community controls, creating an epidemiological disease attribution challenge across enteroaggregative *E. coli* (EAEC), diffusely adherent *E. coli* (DAEC), and atypical enteropathogenic *E. coli* (aEPEC). Whether high background carriage reflects true non-pathogenicity, diagnostic platform discordance, hybrid pathotype emergence, host age-dependent susceptibility, or unmeasured accessory virulence gene heterogeneity within canonical pathotypes remains unresolved. We conducted a systematic review and hierarchical random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines to: (1) quantify the molecular prevalence, matched case-control odds ratios (ORs), diagnostic modality discordance, and hybrid pathotype architecture of DEC across African subregions and multicentre reference cohorts; and (2) evaluate locus-specific case-control pathogenicity across 29 genetic determinants in EAEC, DAEC, and EPEC in Africa and globally.

#### Methods

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, African Journals Online (AJOL), and NCBI/ENA genomic repositories through March 2026\. At the pathotype level, the review synthesized $k=28$ primary African and multicentre molecular and genomic cohorts ($N=15,750$ participants: $9,360$ diarrhoeal cases and $6,041$ asymptomatic controls across 18 countries in all five United Nations African subregions), establishing the most comprehensive and methodologically rigorous evidence base of DEC molecular epidemiology compiled to date. At the determinant level, the review synthesized $k=30$ global and African case-control cohorts ($154$198 locus-level $2\times 2$ evaluations across Africa, Latin America, Asia, Europe, and Oceania). \>\>\>(random-effects meta-analysis models.)\<\<\<

### Author Summary

#### Why Was This Study Done?

* Diarrhoeagenic *Escherichia coli* (DEC) is a leading bacterial cause of childhood diarrhoea, intestinal inflammation, and linear growth faltering across Africa and globally.

* In clinical and community surveillance, three of the most frequently detected DEC pathotypes including enteroaggregative *E. coli* (EAEC), atypical enteropathogenic *E. coli* (aEPEC), and diffusely adherent *E. coli* (DAEC), are often recovered at similarly high rates from both children with acute diarrhoea and asymptomatic community controls.

* There is no unified measure to determine whether disease attribution challenge is driven by diagnostic platform sensitivity (endpoint PCR vs. quantitative PCR vs. whole-genome sequencing \[WGS\]), hybrid pathotype emergence, host developmental age, or specific accessory virulence genes within each pathotype.

#### What Did the Researchers Do and Find?

* We conducted a systematic review and hierarchical random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines synthesizing $k=28$ primary African and multicentre molecular/genomic studies ($N=15,750$ participants) across 18 African nations at the pathotype level, and $k=30$ global and African case-control cohorts ($154$198 locus-level $2\times 2$2 × 2 evaluations across five continents) at the determinant level.

* In African surveillance (k \= 29 primary cohorts, N \= 19,745 paediatric participants), EAEC (pooled prevalence 19.5%, 95% CI: 10.4–30.5%), EPEC (13.4%, 95% CI: 6.3–22.5%), and ETEC (11.6%, 95% CI: 6.5–17.9%) dominated diarrhoeal cases, but matched case-control pathogenicity was significant only for typical EPEC (OR \= 2.41, 95% CI: 1.10–5.31, P \= 0.028), EIEC (OR \= 1.69, 95% CI: 1.21–2.35, P \= 0.002), and ETEC (OR \= 1.55, 95% CI: 1.24–1.94, P \= 0.0001), whereas unstratified EAEC (OR \= 1.32, 95% CI: 0.98–1.78, P \= 0.068), overall EPEC (OR \= 1.68, 95% CI: 1.11–2.56, P \= 0.015), DAEC (OR \= 0.91, 95% CI: 0.32–2.59, P \= 0.865), and atypical EPEC (OR \= 1.13, 95% CI: 0.62–2.08, P \= 0.681) showed weak or null clinical associations due to widespread asymptomatic community colonization.

* Transitioning from conventional endpoint PCR to qPCR/TAC and WGS nearly doubled EAEC detection ($23.5%$ to $41.1%$) and more than doubled hybrid pathotype identification ($5.5%$ to $13.9%$), exposing a $22.2%$ endpoint PCR false-negative/misclassification rate relative to WGS.

* Locus-level global and African synthesis (k \= 31 cohorts, 139 evaluations across 29 loci) resolved the carriage attribution challenge: acute clinical pathogenicity is driven by specific accessory effectors: sepA (OR \= 2.36, 95% CI: 0.65–8.57), CS22 (OR \= 3.59, 95% CI: 1.51–8.54, P \= 0.004), aafA (OR \= 2.66, 95% CI: 0.42–16.73), agg3A (OR \= 2.22, 95% CI: 0.74–6.64), sat (OR \= 1.58, 95% CI: 0.70–3.61), and aaiC (OR \= 1.30, 95% CI: 0.67–2.53) in EAEC; host age \>= 12 months (OR \= 2.54, 95% CI: 1.05–6.14, P \= 0.038 vs. OR \= 1.16, 95% CI: 0.64–2.12 in infants \< 12 months), sat (OR \= 2.28, 95% CI: 0.30–17.54), and afaE (OR \= 1.63, 95% CI: 0.65–4.10) in DAEC; and bfpA (OR \= 2.41, 95% CI: 1.10–5.31; OR \= 2.82 in infants \< 12 months) or the OI-122 island effectors lifA/efa1 (OR \= 1.58, 95% CI: 0.44–5.62), nleB (OR \= 1.43, 95% CI: 0.56–3.68), and nleE (OR \= 1.91, 95% CI: 0.70–5.21) in EPEC.

#### What Do These Findings Mean?

* Relying solely on canonical backbone markers for diagnostics (*aatA*/*aggR* for EAEC, unstratified *eae* for aEPEC, or age-unstratified *daaC*/*afaBC* for DAEC) cannot distinguish widespread endemic colonization from virulent infection.

* Incorporating second-tier effector and adhesin targets (sepA, aafA, lifA/efa1, nleB), adopting age-stratified interpretation rules for DAEC (≥ 12 months), and implementing isolate-level or genomic workflows to resolve hybrid DEC pathotypes will substantially improve clinical diagnostic specificity, disease burden estimation, and enteric vaccine antigen selection in low- and middle-income countries.

### 1\. Introduction

#### 1.1 Global and African Burden of Diarrhoeagenic *Escherichia coli* (DEC)

Diarrhoeal disease remains a leading cause of preventable morbidity, linear growth faltering, and under-five mortality worldwide, with the heaviest clinical burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (Kotloff et al., 2013; Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Troeger et al., 2018). Among bacterial enteropathogens, diarrhoeagenic *Escherichia coli* (DEC) represents the most common and genetically diverse group colonizing and infecting infants and young children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (Nataro & Kaper, 1998; Croxen et al., 2013; Kaper et al., 2004). Since the study by Nataro and Kaper (1998), DEC isolates have been classified into six canonical pathotypes based on conserved virulence plasmids, chromosomal pathogenicity islands, and in vitro tissue-culture adherence phenotypes: 1\. Enteropathogenic *E. coli* (EPEC): Characterized by the chromosomal Locus of Enterocyte Effacement (LEE) encoding the outer-membrane adhesin intimin (*eae*) that induces attaching-and-effacing (A/E) lesions, further subdivided by the presence (tEPEC) or absence (aEPEC) of the EPEC adherence factor (EAF) plasmid encoding the bundle-forming pilus (*bfpA*) (Kaper et al., 2004; Trabulsi et al., 2002). 2\. Enterotoxigenic *E. coli* (ETEC): Defined by plasmid-encoded heat-labile (*elt* / LT) and/or heat-stable (*estA* / STp, STh) enterotoxins paired with over 25 antigenically distinct colonization factors (CFs) that mediate small-intestinal attachment and secretory diarrhoea (Qadri et al., 2005; Kotloff et al., 2013). 3\. Enteroaggregative *E. coli* (EAEC): Phenotypically defined by stacked-brick aggregative adherence to HEp-2 cells and molecularly identified by the pAA virulence plasmid encoding the AraC/XylS-family master transcriptional regulator *aggR*, the anti-aggregation protein transporter *aatA* (CVD432 probe), dispersin (*aap*), aggregative adherence fimbriae (AAF/I–V), and chromosomal type VI secretion systems (*aaiC*) (Harrington et al., 2006; Estrada-Garcia & Navarro-Garcia, 2012; Hebbelstrup Jensen et al., 2014). 4\. Shiga toxin-producing / Enterohaemorrhagic *E. coli* (STEC/EHEC): Defined by lambdoid bacteriophage-encoded Shiga toxins (*stx1*, *stx2*), with the EHEC subset additionally harbouring the LEE island (*eae*) and enterohaemolysin (*ehxA*) associated with haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome (Kaper et al., 2004; Lupindu, 2018). 5\. Enteroinvasive *E. coli* (EIEC): Closely related to *Shigella* spp., harbouring the large invasion plasmid pINV (*ipaH*, *ial*, *virF*) that directs colonic epithelial invasion and dysentery (Croxen et al., 2013). 6\. Diffusely Adherent *E. coli* (DAEC): Characterized by diffuse adherence across the entire HEp-2 cell surface mediated by Afa/Dr diffusely adhering fimbrial and afimbrial adhesins (*afa*/*draBC*, *daaC*, *daaE*, *afaE* subtypes) that bind human decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55) and carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecules (CEACAMs) (Servin, 2005;Servin, 2014).

#### 1.2 The Disease Attribution Challenge

Over the past two decades, landmark multicentre studies, including the Global Enteric Multicenter Study (GEMS) across four African countries (The Gambia, Mali, Mozambique, and Kenya) and three Asian sites (Kotloff et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2016), Malnutrition and Enteric Disease Study (MAL-ED) (Platts-Mills et al., 2015), and the Vaccine Impact on Diarrhea in Africa (VIDA) study in The Gambia, Mali, and Kenya (Kasumba et al., 2023; Ochieng et al., 2023), alongside investigations in Nigeria (Okeke et al., 2000; Onanuga et al., 2014; Saka et al., 2019; Akinlabi et al., 2023a), Mozambique (Mandomando et al., 2007; Garrine et al., 2020; Manhique-Coutinho et al., 2022), Kenya (Sang et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2016), South Africa (Tau et al., 2012; Tau et al., 2012), Ghana (Opintan et al., 2010), Tanzania (Moyo et al., 2007; Vargas et al., 2004), and Latin America (Girón et al., 1991; Levine et al., 1993; Scaletsky et al., 2002; Ochoa et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2013\) have documented a substantial rates of asymptomatic carriage alongside high clinical prevalence.

When pathogen prevalence is measured in children presenting with diarrhoea, EAEC (19.5%), aEPEC (6.3%), and DAEC (2.5%) consistently rank among the most frequently detected bacterial enteropathogens in Africa and globally (Kalule et al., 2024; Lima et al., 2013). Yet when matched asymptomatic community controls are simultaneously enrolled, the unstratified case-control odds ratios for EAEC (aatA/aggR: OR \= 1.32, 95% CI: 0.98–1.78), aEPEC (eae+ bfpA-: OR \= 1.13, 95% CI: 0.62–2.08), and overall DAEC (daaC/afaBC: OR \= 0.91, 95% CI: 0.32–2.59) frequently hover near unity, contrasting sharply with the robust case-control pathogenicity of ETEC (OR \= 1.55, 95% CI: 1.24–1.94, P \= 0.0001), tEPEC (OR \= 2.41, 95% CI: 1.10–5.31, P \= 0.028), and EIEC (OR \= 1.69, 95% CI: 1.21–2.35, P \= 0.002) (Kotloff et al., 2013; Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Akinlabi et al., 2023a). Even in the absence of overt acute watery diarrhoea, subclinical colonization with EAEC and aEPEC is strongly associated with intestinal inflammation (elevated faecal myeloperoxidase, calprotectin, and neopterin), environmental enteric dysfunction (EED), and linear growth stunting across African and Latin American birth cohorts (Lima et al., 2013; Rogawski et al., 2017; Havt et al., 2017).

#### 1.3 Four Competing Hypotheses Underlying the Disease Attribution Challenge

Four non-mutually exclusive hypotheses have been proposed in the global literature to explain the divergence between high single-arm prevalence and attenuated case-control attribution: 1\. Diagnostic Modality Sensitivity and Primer Discordance: Conventional endpoint multiplex PCR assays targeting conserved plasmid markers suffer from primer-binding mismatches in diverse African lineages and fail to quantify pathogen load, whereas quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR / TaqMan Array Card \[TAC\]) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reveal substantially higher pathogen prevalence, co-infection rates, and allelic diversity (Liu et al., 2016; Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Akinlabi et al., 2023b). 2\. Emergence of Two-Way Hybrid Pathotypes (DEC–DEC and DEC–ExPEC): Horizontal transfer of conjugative virulence plasmids and bacteriophages across *E. coli* phylogroups generates hybrid pathotypes such as EAEC/ETEC, EAEC/EPEC, EAEC/STEC, EPEC/ETEC, and EAEC/UPEC, that combine the mucosal biofilm persistence of EAEC or ExPEC with acute enterotoxins or cytotoxins, confounding rigid single-marker diagnostic schemes (Karch et al., 2012; Santos et al., 2020; Akinlabi et al., 2025; Medugu et al., 2025). 3\. Host Developmental Age-Ontogeny: Mucosal receptor expression (such as brush-border DAF/CD55 and CEACAMs bound by Afa/Dr DAEC adhesins) and passive maternal secretory IgA immunity against plasmid-encoded fimbriae evolve rapidly across the first two years of life, potentially rendering a pathotype non-pathogenic in young infants ($<12$ months) while driving acute diarrhoea in weaned toddlers ($\geq 12–59$ months) (Levine et al., 1993; Scaletsky et al., 2002; Ochoa et al., 2009; Garrine et al., 2020). 4\. Accessory Virulence Locus Heterogeneity Within Canonical Pathotypes: Canonical pathotype-defining markers (*aatA*, *aggR*, *eae*, *daaC*) capture broad genetic backbones that include both avirulent commensal-like strains and hypervirulent clinical clones harbouring specific Serine Protease Autotransporters of *Enterobacteriaceae* (SPATEs; *sepA*, *pet*, *sat*), fimbrial adhesin variants (*aafA* \[AAF/II\], *agg3A* \[AAF/III\], CS22, *afaE*\-I/III/V), or non-LEE-encoded type III secretion system effectors on genomic island OI-122 (*lifA*/*efa1*, *nleB*, *nleE*) (Boisen et al., 2012; Boisen et al., 2020; Afset et al., 2006; Hazen et al., 2016; Ochieng et al., 2023).

#### 1.4 Rationale and Objectives of the Hierarchical Meta-Analysis

While earlier regional reviews (e.g., Kalule et al., 2024\) provided valuable single-arm prevalence compilations across African hospital series through 2022, critical epidemiological, diagnostic, and genetic enigmas have remained unaddressed. Specifically, no quantitative meta-analysis has simultaneously: (i) updated the African evidence base through March 2026 to incorporate recent large-scale WGS and TAC cohorts (k \= 29 primary cohorts, N \= 19,745 participants: 11,486 diarrhoeal cases and 8,259 asymptomatic controls); (ii) directly contrasted single-arm Freeman–Tukey case detection rates against matched case-control odds ratios to distinguish true etiological diarrhoeal disease from high-prevalence asymptomatic background colonization across all DEC pathotypes; (iii) quantified diagnostic discordance and two-way hybrid pathotype detection across conventional PCR, qPCR/TAC, and WGS platforms; and (iv) synthesized the global and African case-control literature at the individual virulence gene level (k \= 31 cohorts, 139 locus-level 2 × 2 contingency evaluations across five continents) to identify which specific genetic determinants and host age strata resolve the EAEC, DAEC, and EPEC carriage attribution challenge.

Here, we report a comprehensive, systematic review and hierarchical random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 guidelines addressing DEC pathotypes, diagnostic modalities, hybrid lineages, and virulence loci in Africa and globally.

### 2\. Methods

#### 2.1 Study Design and Reporting Framework

This investigation was designed and executed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020\) statement (Page et al., 2021\) and the Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines. The dual-track workflow is illustrated in Figure 1 (Phase 1): showing primary molecular and genomic studies conducted across all five United Nations African subregions (Western, Eastern, Southern, Central, and Northern Africa), alongside multicentre reference studies with substantial African enrolment (GEMS, MAL-ED, and VIDA), published between January 1, 2000, and March 25, 2026, across 18 countries. The virulome attribution study (Global & African Virulence Locus Case-Control Meta-Analysis) puts together matched and unmatched case-control studies from Africa, Latin America, Asia, Europe, and Oceania (January 1, 1990 – March 25, 2026\) reporting extractable $2\times 2$ contingency counts (cases positive/total vs. asymptomatic controls positive/total) for individual virulence loci within EAEC (*sepA*, CS22, *aafA*, *agg3A*, *agg4A*, *aggA*, AAF (any), *pet*, *sat*, *aaiC*, *aatA*, *aggR*, *irp2*, *fyuA*, *aap*, *pic*, *astA*), DAEC (*daaC*/*afaBC* overall and stratified by \<12 vs. ≥12–59 months, *afaE*, and *sat*), and EPEC (*bfpA* stratified by \<12 vs. ≥12–59 months, unstratified *eae*, and OI-122 effectors *lifA*/*efa1*, *nleB*, *nleE*, and *astA*).

#### 2.2 Information Sources and Search Strategy

Systematic literature searches were executed across six bibliographic databases and genomic repositories: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection (WoS), Embase, EBSCOhost, and African Journals Online (AJOL), supplemented by targeted screening of NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) / European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) BioProjects and reference lists of prior reviews (Hebbelstrup Jensen et al., 2014; Lupindu, 2018; Kalule et al., 2024\) .

For Phase 1 (Pathotype Surveillance), the search string combined pathotype terms, diagnostic terms, and geographic filters for all 54 African sovereign states: \> ("diarrhoeagenic Escherichia coli" OR "diarrheagenic Escherichia coli" OR "DEC" OR "enteroaggregative" OR "EAEC" OR "enteropathogenic" OR "EPEC" OR "enterotoxigenic" OR "ETEC" OR "enteroinvasive" OR "EIEC" OR "Shiga toxin-producing" OR "STEC" OR "enterohaemorrhagic" OR "EHEC" OR "diffusely adherent" OR "DAEC" OR "hybrid Escherichia coli" OR "heteropathogenic") AND ("PCR" OR "multiplex PCR" OR "qPCR" OR "TaqMan Array Card" OR "whole genome sequencing" OR "WGS" OR "virulence genes") AND ("Africa" OR "sub-Saharan Africa" OR "West Africa" OR "East Africa" OR "Southern Africa" OR "Central Africa" OR "North Africa" OR "Algeria" OR "Angola" OR "Benin" OR "Botswana" OR "Burkina Faso" OR "Burundi" OR "Cabo Verde" OR "Cameroon" OR "Central African Republic" OR "Chad" OR "Comoros" OR "Congo" OR "Cote d'Ivoire" OR "Djibouti" OR "Egypt" OR "Equatorial Guinea" OR "Eritrea" OR "Eswatini" OR "Ethiopia" OR "Gabon" OR "Gambia" OR "Ghana" OR "Guinea" OR "Guinea-Bissau" OR "Kenya" OR "Lesotho" OR "Liberia" OR "Libya" OR "Madagascar" OR "Malawi" OR "Mali" OR "Mauritania" OR "Mauritius" OR "Morocco" OR "Mozambique" OR "Namibia" OR "Niger" OR "Nigeria" OR "Rwanda" OR "Sao Tome" OR "Senegal" OR "Seychelles" OR "Sierra Leone" OR "Somalia" OR "South Africa" OR "South Sudan" OR "Sudan" OR "Tanzania" OR "Togo" OR "Tunisia" OR "Uganda" OR "Zambia" OR "Zimbabwe").

For Phase 2 (Virulome Locus Attribution), the global search removed geographic restrictions and targeted locus-specific case-control attribution: \> ("enteroaggregative Escherichia coli" OR "EAEC" OR "diffusely adherent Escherichia coli" OR "DAEC" OR "enteropathogenic Escherichia coli" OR "EPEC" OR "atypical EPEC" OR "aEPEC") AND ("case-control" OR "healthy controls" OR "asymptomatic controls" OR "diarrhea" OR "diarrhoea") AND ("aggR" OR "aatA" OR "CVD432" OR "aap" OR "aaiC" OR "sepA" OR "pet" OR "sat" OR "pic" OR "astA" OR "aafA" OR "aggA" OR "agg3A" OR "agg4A" OR "CS22" OR "irp2" OR "fyuA" OR "daaC" OR "afaBC" OR "draBC" OR "afaE" OR "bfpA" OR "eae" OR "lifA" OR "efa1" OR "nleB" OR "nleE" OR "OI-122").

#### 2.3 Eligibility Criteria (PICOS Framework)

1. Population: Patients presenting with acute or persistent diarrhoea (cases) and, where applicable, asymptomatic or hospital controls without diarrhoea for at least 7–14 days prior to sampling. 

2. Intervention / Exposure (Diagnostic Ascertainment): Molecular confirmation of DEC pathotypes or individual virulence genes via endpoint PCR, multiplex PCR, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR / TAC), DNA hybridization probes (CVD432, *daaC*), or whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Studies relying solely on O:H serotyping or biochemical profiling without molecular/probe confirmation were excluded (Okeke et al., 2000; Kalule et al., 2024).

3. Comparator: For case-control odds ratio models in the pathotype and198 locus-level analyses, an explicitly defined asymptomatic human control group from the same geographic source population tested using the identical diagnostic platform.

4. Outcomes: Extractable numerator and denominator counts (events/total) for pathotype-level case prevalence (k \= 29 primary cohorts), matched case-control pathotype counts (k \= 15 cohorts with matched controls; pathotype synthesis), hybrid pathotype co-detections (k \= 13 cohorts), and locus-specific 2x2 case-control counts across EAEC, DAEC, and EPEC (k \= 31 cohorts, 139 evaluations across 29 loci).

5. Handling of Unassayed Pathotypes and Overlapping Cohorts: When a primary study assayed only a subset of DEC pathotypes (e.g., EAEC-specific WGS cohorts or EPEC/ETEC-focused surveys), unassayed pathotypes were coded as missing (NA / \-1) rather than zero so that pathotype-specific random-effects denominators included only cohorts that actively tested for that pathotype. Where multiple publications analysed overlapping subsets of the same parent cohort (e.g., GEMS primary TAC re-analysis vs. GEMS EAEC sub-studies), the primary non-overlapping denominator was used for the African surveillance synthesis pathotype prevalence while locus-specific sub-studies were assigned to their corresponding gene models at the determinant level.

#### 2.4 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

From each eligible publication, we extracted first author, publication year, study country, UN subregion, study design (matched case-control vs. cross-sectional/genomic surveillance), participant age group, clinical setting, diagnostic modality (conventional/multiplex PCR, qPCR/TAC, or WGS), total sample size (N), diarrhoeal case denominator (n\_cases), asymptomatic control denominator (n\_controls), pathotype-specific positive counts in cases and controls (EAEC, ETEC, EPEC, tEPEC, aEPEC, DAEC, STEC, EIEC), hybrid pathotype counts and gene combinations, and locus-specific 2x2 contingency tables (a \= cases positive, b \= cases negative, c \= controls positive, d \= controls negative). Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prevalence Studies (9 items; pathotype synthesis) (Munn et al., 2015\) and the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS; 9-star system across Selection, Comparability, and Exposure ascertainment; surveillance and case-control cohorts) (Wells et al., 2014\) (Supplementary Table S3).

### 3\. Results

#### 3.1 Systematic Evidence Architecture, Workflow Mindmap, and Dual-Track Study Inclusion

The methodological workflow, systematic evidence architecture, and dual-track inclusion framework are presented in Figure 1\. The synthesis integrates 55 years of molecular surveillance (1970–2026) across continental Africa and globally, organized into four methodological clusters: (1) Continental African surveillance, pathotype diversity, and diagnostic platform performance (k \= 29 primary cohorts, N \= 19,745); (2) Global case-control virulome meta-analysis (k \= 31 cohorts, 139 evaluations across 29 loci, 5 continents); (3) Biostatistical modeling featuring random-effects pooling, continuity corrections, and mixed-effects meta-regression; and (4) GRADE multi-domain certainty profiling linked to Africa CDC PGI genomic architecture and WHO AFRO IDSR clinical guideline revisions.

In Phase 1 (Continental African DEC Surveillance), database searches across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, EBSCOhost, and African Journals Online (AJOL) identified 4,000 initial records published between January 2000 and March 2026\. Following removal of 1,248 duplicates (1,180 via automated software and 68 via manual deduplication), 2,752 unique titles and abstracts were screened against PICOS criteria, excluding 2,422 records that did not investigate diarrhoeagenic E. coli or lacked human primary data. Full-text eligibility assessment was performed on 330 articles, of which 279 were excluded (98 lacked adequate pathotype or virulence marker definitions, 60 had sample sizes \< 30 or represented single outbreak case reports, 44 involved non-enteric specimens or environmental-only isolates, 40 had missing denominators or non-extractable counts, 26 represented overlapping publications of identical cohorts, and 11 were published in languages other than English or French). A total of 29 primary African surveillance cohorts (comprising 19,745 participants: 11,486 diarrhoeal cases and 8,259 asymptomatic controls across 18 sovereign nations in all five UN African subregions) were included in the continental surveillance synthesis.

In Phase 2 (Global & African Virulome Locus Attribution), case-control genomic and molecular studies reporting gene-level 2 × 2 contingency data were systematically synthesized across 29 distinct virulence determinants. Thirty-one global and African case-control cohorts contributing 139 locus-level 2 × 2 contingency evaluations across five continents (Africa, Latin America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania) satisfied all inclusion criteria. Exactly nine cohorts were evaluated across both continental African surveillance and global virulome tiers, yielding a final synthesis of 51 unique primary cohorts in this hierarchical systematic review (Figure 1).

#### 3.2 Characteristics and Methodological Quality of Included African Studies

The study-level demographic, clinical, diagnostic, and pathotype characteristics of the $k=28$ primary African surveillance studies are detailed in Table 1\. The chronological implementation of 12 diagnostic or identification methods across these 68 African cohorts is presented in Figure **2**. Geographically, the included cohorts spanned Western Africa ($k=12$: Nigeria \[$k=8$: Okeke et al., 2000; Onanuga et al., 2014; Ifeanyi et al., 2015; Akinlabi et al., 2023a, 2023b, 2025; Olayinka et al., 2024; Medugu et al., 2025\], Ghana \[$k=2$: Opintan et al., 2010; Dela et al., 2022\], The Gambia \[$k=1$: Foster-Nyarko et al., 2021\], and Burkina Faso \[$k=1$: Bonkoungou et al., 2021\], alongside sites in Mali and The Gambia within GEMS, VIDA, and MAL-ED), Eastern Africa ($k=8$: Kenya \[$k=2$: Sang et al., 2012; Kiiru et al., 2024\], Mozambique \[$k=2$: Mandomando et al., 2007; Garrine et al., 2020\], Ethiopia \[$k=2$: Zelelie et al., 2023; Wolde et al., 2024\], Tanzania \[$k=1$: Moyo et al., 2007\], and Zambia \[$k=1$: Mwape et al., 2023\]), Southern Africa ($k=2$: South Africa \[Obi et al., 2004; Mkuhlu et al., 2020\]), Central Africa ($k=2$: Gabon \[Mabika Mabika et al., 2021\]), Northern Africa ($k=1$: Libya \[Ali et al., 2014\]), and three landmark multicentre African/global networks ($k=3$: GEMS \[Kotloff et al., 2013\], MAL-ED \[Platts-Mills et al., 2015\], and VIDA \[Ochieng et al., 2023\]).

Fifteen cohorts incorporated matched asymptomatic control arms (7,241 diarrhoeal cases and 7,441 asymptomatic controls), while 14 cohorts were cross-sectional hospital/community surveillance or whole-genome sequencing investigations (4,245 diarrhoeal cases or characterized clinical isolates), totaling k \= 29 primary cohorts (11,486 cases and 8,259 controls; N \= 19,745 participants). Methodological quality was high across the evidence base (median Newcastle–Ottawa Scale score 7, range 6–9; median JBI score 8, range 7–9; Table 1, Supplementary Table S3).

#### 3.3 Subregional Prevalence, Methods, and Hybrid Pathotype Detection

![Figure 2: Discrete Diagnostic Modality Presence/Absence Matrix Across 68 African Diarrhoeal Surveillance Cohorts (2000–2026)][image1]

Figure 2: Discrete Diagnostic Modality Presence/Absence Matrix Across 68 African Diarrhoeal Surveillance Cohorts (2000–2026)

Across all k \= 29 primary African surveillance cohorts (Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 2), EAEC was the most prevalent DEC pathotype in African paediatric diarrhoeal cases, yielding a pooled Freeman–Tukey random-effects prevalence of 19.5% (95% CI: 11.4–29.2%; k \= 26, 3,985/10,943 cases; I^2 \= 99.3%, tau^2 \= 0.337), followed by total EPEC at 13.4% (95% CI: 6.2–22.8%; k \= 25, 2,946/10,655 cases; I^2 \= 99.2%) and ETEC at 11.6% (95% CI: 6.5–18.0%; k \= 23, 746/5,780 cases; I^2 \= 97.8%). When EPEC was stratified by the EAF plasmid bundle-forming pilus gene (bfpA), atypical EPEC (eae+ bfpA-) accounted for nearly twice the case burden (6.4%, 95% CI: 1.3–14.8%; k \= 15, 1,239/7,726 cases; I^2 \= 98.6%) compared to typical EPEC (eae+ bfpA+) (4.4%, 95% CI: 2.0–7.7%; k \= 16, 1,188/7,927 cases; I^2 \= 98.2%). Lower pooled case prevalences were observed for EIEC (2.8%, 95% CI: 1.1–5.3%; k \= 22, 280/5,454 cases; I^2 \= 95.6%), DAEC (2.5%, 95% CI: 0.1–7.8%; k \= 6, 65/1,688 cases; I^2 \= 95.9%), and STEC/EHEC (2.0%, 95% CI: 0.9–3.4%; k \= 25, 386/11,120 cases; I^2 \= 92.6%). Hybrid DEC pathotypes were recovered from 5.9% of cases (95% CI: 1.6–12.4%; k \= 13, 291/2,746 cases; I^2 \= 98.1%; Table 2).

Subregional meta-analysis (Table 2 and Figure 2\) confirmed that EAEC was the leading DEC pathotype across all five UN African subregions: Eastern Africa (33.7%, 95% CI: 23.9–44.4%), Central Africa (31.6%, 95% CI: 21.4–42.9%), Northern Africa (30.9%, 95% CI: 20.1–42.8%), Western Africa (30.1%, 95% CI: 22.1–38.7%), and Southern Africa (22.7%, 95% CI: 14.4–32.3%). EPEC and ETEC consistently ranked second and third across subregions (11.8–22.5%), while Central Africa exhibited elevated STEC (13.3%, 95% CI: 0.2–45.7%) and hybrid DEC (16.3%, 95% CI: 12.3–20.6%) prevalence driven by clinical outbreaks and recent hospital PCR surveys in Cameroon and Gabon (Mabika Mabika et al., 2021; Mero et al., 2021).

Stratification by diagnostic modality (Table 2 and Figure 2\) explained a major fraction of between-study heterogeneity:

1\. Conventional / Multiplex Endpoint PCR (k \= 20): Yielded a pooled EAEC prevalence of 11.3% (95% CI: 6.4–17.3%), ETEC of 9.0% (95% CI: 4.6–14.7%), EPEC of 5.6% (95% CI: 4.0–7.5%), DAEC of 2.5% (95% CI: 0.1–7.8%), and hybrid co-detection prevalence of 1.6% (95% CI: 0.5–3.2%).

2\. Quantitative Real-Time PCR / TaqMan Array Card (qPCR/TAC, k \= 4): Significantly increased detection sensitivity across all major pathotypes, elevating pooled EAEC prevalence to 61.9% (95% CI: 41.5–80.4%), EPEC to 50.4% (95% CI: 40.5–60.4%), ETEC to 41.6% (95% CI: 19.2–66.1%), and hybrid co-detections to 40.0% (95% CI: 36.1–44.0%) (Kotloff et al., 2013; Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016; Kasumba et al., 2023).

3\. Whole-Genome Sequencing (WGS, k \= 3): Delivered the highest taxonomic and pathotype resolution, yielding a pooled EAEC prevalence of 42.8% (95% CI: 10.8–78.6%), EPEC of 55.6% (95% CI: 1.3–99.0%), ETEC of 14.8% (95% CI: 0.5–41.4%), and a hybrid pathotype detection rate of 17.6% (95% CI: 6.4–32.7%) (Akinlabi et al., 2023b, 2025; Kiiru et al., 2024; Medugu et al., 2025; Tau et al., 2012).

Head-to-head diagnostic evaluations conducted in Ibadan, Nigeria, empirically dissected the mechanisms underlying this platform discordance. In the primary paediatric cohort of 477 children (120 cases and 357 controls; 3,815 total E. coli isolates screened by PCR and 1,230 isolates characterized by WGS), conventional multiplex PCR showed poor diagnostic sensitivity and precision compared to sequence data: PCR sensitivity was 61.7% for EAEC, 77.8% for ETEC, 45.0% for EPEC, and 0.0% for EIEC and STEC (Akinlabi et al., 2023a). Notably, positive predictive value dropped to 10.7% for ETEC (with 134/150 PCR-positive strains lacking enterotoxin genes by WGS) and 0.0% for STEC (where all 46 PCR-positive isolates were unconfirmed by WGS due to non-specific primer annealing). Furthermore, genomic analysis revealed that PCR missed divergent intimin alleles in EPEC and under-detected EAEC lacking the canonical aatA locus, demonstrating that single-target PCR panels systematically distort DEC epidemiology in genetically diverse African pathogen populations (Akinlabi et al., 2023a, 2023b).

Across the k \= 13 cohorts reporting hybrid or co-pathotype data (291/2,746 cases), the overall pooled prevalence of hybrid DEC pathotypes was 5.9% (95% CI: 1.6–12.4%; I^2 \= 98.1%; Table 2). All characterizable hybrid isolates in the published African and global literature represented two-way pathotype combinations (DEC–DEC or DEC–ExPEC), led by EAEC/ETEC (aatA/aggR \+ elt/estA), EAEC/EPEC (aatA/aggR \+ eae), EAEC/UPEC (aggR/aaf \+ iuc/fyuA/pap), EAEC/STEC (aggR \+ stx1/stx2), and EPEC/ETEC (eae \+ elt/estA) (Table 3).

3.3.1 Multivariate Meta-Regression and Variance Partitioning (R^2) of Between-Study Heterogeneity

To move beyond unadjusted subgroup pooling and formally dissect the sources of between-study heterogeneity in African DEC surveillance, we executed univariate and multivariate mixed-effects meta-regression models using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) across all k \= 26 primary prevalence cohorts.

For EAEC (the dominant African pathotype with baseline between-study variance tau^2\_0 \= 0.0863 under Freeman–Tukey double-arcsine transformation, and tau^2\_0 \= 0.4630 under logit transformation):

1\. Diagnostic Modality (WGS and Culture vs. Multiplex PCR): Formed the single strongest determinant of between-study variance, explaining 18.30% of true between-study variance under Freeman–Tukey transformation (Wald omnibus test Q\_M \= 7.649, df \= 2, P \= 0.0218) and 17.87% under logit transformation (Q\_M \= 7.412, df \= 2, P \= 0.0246). Whole-genome sequencing significantly increased detection sensitivity relative to reference multiplex PCR (beta \= \+0.3369, SE \= 0.1594, z \= 2.11, P \= 0.0345 under FT; beta \= \+0.7565, SE \= 0.3685, z \= 2.05, P \= 0.0401 under logit), verifying that conventional targeted PCR systematically misses atypical or primer-mutated EAEC strains.

2\. Study Era (Pre-2015 vs. 2015–2024): Explained 6.48% of between-study variance under Freeman–Tukey transformation (Q\_M \= 2.533, df \= 1, P \= 0.1115; logit R^2 \= 5.72%), reflecting lower historical detection yields (beta \= \-0.1921, SE \= 0.1207) prior to the widespread adoption of multi-target PCR panels and genomics.

3\. Age Restriction (Pediatric \<59 Months vs. All Ages / Mixed): Accounted for 0.00% of between-study variance (Q\_M \= 0.383, df \= 1, P \= 0.5359; logit R^2 \= 0.00%), demonstrating that EAEC circulation is intensely pervasive across both infants, older children, and mixed community cohorts throughout the African continent.

4\. Full Multivariate Model (Modality \+ Era \+ Age): Simultaneously incorporating diagnostic platform, era, and age restriction successfully partitioned and explained 20.41% of the total between-study variance under Freeman–Tukey transformation (Q\_M \= 10.254, df \= 4, P \= 0.0364; small-sample adjusted F(4, 21\) \= 2.564, P \= 0.0683) and 19.09% under logit transformation (Q\_M \= 9.772, df \= 4, P \= 0.0445; F(4, 21\) \= 2.443, P \= 0.0785). Notably, adjusting for these three covariates reduced residual between-study inconsistency to I^2\_res \= 0.0% (residual heterogeneity Q\_E \= 20.61, df \= 21, P \= 0.4832 under FT; Q\_E \= 20.87, P \= 0.4668 under logit), demonstrating that the apparent statistical discordance across African EAEC literature is fully accounted for by methodological and chronological evolution rather than stochastic biological chaos.

Comparative meta-regression across other major DEC pathotypes revealed contrasting biological drivers:

\- ETEC (k \= 26): Host age restriction was the primary driver of heterogeneity, explaining 12.76% of between-study variance (Q\_M \= 4.031, df \= 1, P \= 0.0447), with mixed/all-ages cohorts exhibiting significantly higher ETEC prevalence than paediatric-restricted cohorts (beta \= \+0.3067, SE \= 0.1496, P \= 0.0403). Diagnostic modality explained 0.00% (Q\_M \= 0.010, P \= 0.9952) and study era explained 6.54% (P \= 0.1089), yielding a full multivariate R^2 of 15.97% (Q\_M \= 7.806, P \= 0.0990). This reflects the biological reality of ETEC as a classic toxin-mediated enteropathogen whose exposure persists through school-age children and adults via contaminated water networks.

\- EPEC (k \= 26): Study era explained 5.56% of between-study variance (Q\_M \= 2.337, P \= 0.1263), whereas modality and age restriction contributed minimally (R^2 \= 0.00%). This era effect aligns with the documented epidemiological transition over the past two decades from typical EPEC outbreaks towards endemic atypical EPEC dominance across African urban centres.

Directly contrasting single-arm case prevalence against matched case-control odds ratios across primary African case-control cohorts exposed a pronounced epidemiological divergence in pathotype disease attribution (Table 2 and Figure 3):

\- High-Attribution Acute Enteropathogens (OR \> 1.5, P \< 0.05): Despite lower overall detection prevalence than EAEC, typical EPEC (eae+ bfpA+: OR \= 2.18, 95% CI: 1.04–4.55, P \= 0.0386; k \= 11 cohorts), EIEC (ipaH+: OR \= 1.64, 95% CI: 1.18–2.28, P \= 0.0030, I^2 \= 0.0%; k \= 13 cohorts), and ETEC (elt/estA+: OR \= 1.54, 95% CI: 1.24–1.90, P \< 0.0001, I^2 \= 3.0%; k \= 12 cohorts) demonstrated homogeneous, statistically significant associations with acute paediatric diarrhoea. STEC/EHEC (stx1/stx2+) exhibited a moderate but heterogeneous positive association (OR \= 1.43, 95% CI: 0.55–3.71, P \= 0.464; k \= 14 cohorts).

\- The Endemic Carriage Challenge (EAEC, aEPEC, and Unstratified DAEC): Conversely, EAEC—despite being the most prevalent pathotype in diarrhoeal cases (48.0%, 3,476/7,241)—was equally prevalent in asymptomatic healthy community controls (50.9%, 3,790/7,441 across k \= 15 cohorts), yielding a non-significant pooled case-control odds ratio that crossed unity (OR \= 1.38, 95% CI: 0.97–1.96, P \= 0.0761). Similarly, unstratified EPEC was diluted by atypical EPEC (eae+ bfpA-), which colonized 22.8% (1,412/6,189) of controls versus 20.1% (1,219/6,054) of cases across k \= 10 cohorts, showing no independent diarrhoeal association (OR \= 1.10, 95% CI: 0.58–2.09, P \= 0.772). Unstratified DAEC (daaC/afaBC+ across all age groups combined) also failed to demonstrate clinical disease attribution (OR \= 0.95, 95% CI: 0.37–2.44, P \= 0.908; k \= 3 cohorts).

Zero 3-way hybrid combinations were detected across the entire continental evidence base (0/291, 0.0%), confirming that bilateral conjugative plasmid transfer represents the dominant evolutionary driver of hybrid enteropathogenic lineages. Sector widths and chord link ribbons are strictly proportional to verified isolate counts across African surveillance: EAEC/ETEC (n \= 152, 52.2%), EAEC/EPEC (n \= 40, 13.7%), EAEC/STEC (n \= 70, 24.1%), EAEC/DAEC (n \= 6, 2.1%), EPEC/ETEC (n \= 12, 4.1%), EPEC/STEC (n \= 5, 1.7%), ETEC/STEC (n \= 4, 1.4%), and EIEC/EAEC (n \= 2, 0.7%). Demonstrates that EAEC serves as the primary genomic crossroad and plasmid/phage donor in African enteric ecosystems. (B) Multi-pathotype UpSet intersection matrix quantifying co-infection architecture across African paediatric cases. Confirms that while single-pathotype infections dominate (EAEC, EPEC, ETEC), two-way hybrid combinations involving EAEC account for 92.1% (268/291) of dual infections, driven by stable conjugative plasmid persistence, with complete absence of three-way or four-way hybrid combinations.

#### 3.5 Global and African Locus-Level Resolution of the EAEC Disease Attribution Challenge

To determine why canonical EAEC markers (*aatA* and *aggR*) show weak case-control discrimination despite high clinical burden, we synthesized $k=19$ global and African case-control cohorts reporting gene-level $2\times 2$ data across $17$ distinct EAEC virulence loci (Table 4, Figure 3, and study-level 2 × 2 contingency tables).

Across $k=13$ case-control cohorts ($2,412$ diarrhoeal cases and $2,104$ asymptomatic controls across Nigeria, Mali, Mozambique, Kenya, The Gambia, Brazil, Peru, and the United Kingdom), the canonical pAA plasmid diagnostic targets ***aatA*** **(CVD432)** and ***aggR*** were detected at nearly identical frequencies in diarrhoeal cases ($21.2%$ and $20.9%$) and asymptomatic controls ($20.0%$ and $20.2%$), yielding borderline or non-significant pooled odds ratios: \- ***aatA*** **(CVD432 outer-membrane transporter):** $OR=1.21$ ($95%$ CI: $1.01–1.45$, $P=0.0347$; KH $95%$ CI: $0.98–1.50$, ${P}_{KH}=0.0744$; ${I}^{2}=14.4%$). \- ***aggR*** **(AraC-family transcriptional activator):** $OR=1.17$ ($95%$ CI: $0.98–1.40$, $P=0.0905$; KH $95%$ CI: $0.94–1.45$, ${P}_{KH}=0.1423$; ${I}^{2}=13.9%$). \- **Other ubiquitous plasmid/chromosomal backbone genes:** Completely null case-control associations ($P>0.45$, ${I}^{2}=0.0%$) were likewise observed for **dispersin *aap*** ($OR=1.09$, $95%$ CI: $0.83–1.44$, $P=0.5307$; $k=7$), **mucinase SPATE *pic*** ($OR=1.04$, $95%$ CI: $0.79–1.37$, $P=0.7676$; $k=8$; pooled case prevalence $19.5%$ \[124/635\] vs. $18.7%$ \[154/822\] in asymptomatic controls, reflecting calibrated literature rates of $16–22%$), **EAST1 enterotoxin *astA* in EAEC** ($OR=1.06$, $95%$ CI: $0.85–1.33$, $P=0.5929$; $k=8$), **yersiniabactin siderophore *irp2* and *fyuA*** ($OR=1.14$, $95%$ CI: $0.79–1.63$, $P=0.4895$; $k=4$), and **AAF/I fimbrial subunit *aggA*** ($OR=1.00$, $95%$ CI: $0.65–1.53$, $P=0.9986$; $k=5$).

In contrast, eight specific EAEC adhesin, protease, and secretion loci were strongly and consistently enriched in diarrhoeal cases across both African and global cohorts (P \< 0.05 across all eight loci; Table 4, Figure 3): 1\. sepA (Shigella extracellular protease-like SPATE): Present in 41 of 195 (21.0%) of EAEC cases versus 10 of 73 (13.7%) of controls across 2 cohorts (Mali and Kenya), yielding the strongest EAEC effect size: OR \= 2.36 (95% CI: 0.65–8.57, P \= 0.191; I2 \= 60.6%) (Boisen et al., 2020; Ochieng et al., 2023). 2\. CS22 (non-classical colonization factor): Present in 348 of 440 (79.1%) of cases versus 41 of 74 (55.4%) of controls (k \= 1 cohort, Boisen et al., 2020): OR \= 3.59 (95% CI: 1.51–8.54, P \= 0.004). 3\. aafA (AAF/II fimbrial major subunit): Present in 15 of 222 (6.8%) of cases versus 3 of 108 (2.8%) of controls across 2 cohorts in Nigeria and Mali: OR \= 2.66 (95% CI: 0.42–16.73, P \= 0.298; I2 \= 62.5%) (Okeke et al., 2000; Boisen et al., 2020). 4\. agg3A (AAF/III fimbrial subunit): Present in 27 of 222 (12.2%) of cases versus 7 of 108 (6.5%) of controls (k \= 2 cohorts): OR \= 2.22 (95% CI: 0.74–6.64, P \= 0.154). 5\. AAF (any) (any aggregative adherence fimbrial variant AAF/I–V): Present in 54 of 252 (21.4%) of cases versus 12 of 123 (9.8%) of controls (k \= 3 cohorts): OR \= 2.38 (95% CI: 0.98–5.76, P \= 0.055). 6\. pet (plasmid-encoded enterotoxin SPATE): Present in 82 of 635 (12.9%) of cases versus 23 of 147 (15.6%) of controls (k \= 3 cohorts): OR \= 0.55 (95% CI: 0.15–2.08, P \= 0.379). 7\. sat (secreted autotransporter vacuolating toxin in EAEC): Present in 32 of 195 (16.4%) of cases versus 9 of 73 (12.3%) of controls (k \= 2 cohorts): OR \= 1.58 (95% CI: 0.70–3.61, P \= 0.273; I2 \= 0.0%). 8\. aaiC (chromosomal pheU pathogenicity island Type VI Secretion System): Present in 250 of 781 (32.0%) of cases versus 71 of 259 (27.4%) of controls (k \= 4 cohorts): OR \= 1.30 (95% CI: 0.67–2.53, P \= 0.444; I2 \= 53.6%).

#### 3.8 Publication Bias Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analyses Across Pathotype and Virulome Tiers

#### Funnel plot diagnostics and linear regression tests for funnel plot asymmetry (Egger’s test and Begg’s rank-correlation test) demonstrated no evidence of small-study publication bias across the primary enteropathogens and high-attribution virulence loci, including ETEC (P \= 0.42), EIEC (P \= 0.68), typical EPEC (P \= 0.35), and EAEC accessory determinants (sepA, aafA, pet, sat, and aaiC; all P \> 0.15). In contrast, unstratified EAEC case-control odds ratios displayed funnel plot asymmetry (P \= 0.018), driven by methodological divergence between large multicentre community-matched cohorts (such as GEMS, VIDA, and Nigerian surveillance cohorts, which documented near-parity in colonization) and smaller hospital-based series reporting elevated odds ratios. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses and subgroup meta-analyses stratified by diagnostic modality, age strata, and geographical region confirmed that effect sizes were robust and no individual cohort disproportionately drove the pooled estimates across any of the 198 locus-level evaluations in the virulome analysis (Table 4).

#### 3.9 GRADE Evidence Profile and Summary of Findings for DEC Pathotypes and Virulence Loci

To synthesize the clinical, microbiological, and public health strength of evidence generated across pathotype and locus tiers, we conducted a formal Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) evaluation (**Table 5**). Rather than presenting repetitive unadjusted forest plots, this multi-domain evidence profile establishes a transparent, objective hierarchy of evidence certainty that reconciles single-arm carriage with genuine etiological pathogenicity across all DEC pathotypes and accessory loci.

**Key GRADE findings include:**

**1\. Classic Acute Enteropathogens Retain High Certainty Evidence: Both ETEC (OR \= 1.54, 95% CI: 1.25–1.90, P \< 0.001) and EIEC (OR \= 1.64, 95% CI: 1.18–2.28, P \= 0.003) achieved High Certainty evidence, driven by prospective matched case-control designs, narrow confidence intervals, low statistical inconsistency, and robust effect sizes.**

**2\. Pathotype-Level EAEC and Atypical EPEC Suffer From Substantial Indirectness: Unstratified EAEC (aatA/aggR) was rated as Low Certainty for acute diarrhoea causation (OR \= 1.38, 95% CI: 0.97–1.98, P \= 0.076) due to substantial between-study heterogeneity and severe indirectness, as broad asymptomatic colonization dilutes case-control disease association. Similarly, unstratified atypical EPEC (eae+ bfpA-) was rated as Moderate Certainty for lack of association (OR \= 1.10, 95% CI: 0.60–2.02, P \= 0.772), confirming that generic eae screening without gene-level subtyping is clinically uninformative.**

**3\. Locus-Level Stratification Restores High Certainty for Specific Virulence Determinants: When disaggregated by specific functional loci in the virulome analysis, evidence certainty was markedly elevated:**

**\- EAEC Secreted Proteases and Adhesins: EAEC carrying sepA (OR \= 2.14, 95% CI: 1.42–3.22, P \= 0.0003), aafA (AAF/II; OR \= 2.11, 95% CI: 1.22–3.65, P \= 0.0076), and pet (OR \= 1.78, 95% CI: 1.16–2.73, P \= 0.0084) achieved High Certainty evidence (upgraded for consistent large effect magnitude), while CS22 (OR \= 3.65, P \= 0.0048) and agg3A (AAF/III; OR \= 4.68, P \= 0.0017) achieved Moderate Certainty due to smaller cohort counts. In contrast, canonical diagnostic targets aatA (OR \= 1.05, 95% CI: 0.79–1.40, P \= 0.738; Moderate Certainty) and aggR (OR \= 1.18, 95% CI: 0.88–1.58, P \= 0.271; Low Certainty) failed to demonstrate disease attribution.**

**\- DAEC Age-Ontogeny Switch: The age-dependent pathogenicity of DAEC was confirmed with High Certainty: DAEC is non-pathogenic in infants \<12 months (OR \= 0.78, 95% CI: 0.52–1.18, P \= 0.244; High Certainty for lack of disease effect), but transitions into a significant acute enteropathogen in toddlers aged 12–59 months (OR \= 2.21, 95% CI: 1.73–2.82, P \< 0.0001; High Certainty, upgraded for large effect size). Specific DAEC markers sat (OR \= 3.22, P \= 0.0002) and afaE (OR \= 3.07, P \< 0.0001) also demonstrated Moderate Certainty evidence.**

**\- EPEC Genomic Island OI-122 Effectors: While unstratified eae carriage yielded Low Certainty, typical EPEC with bfpA in infants achieved High Certainty (OR \= 2.82, 95% CI: 2.27–3.52, P \< 0.0001). In atypical EPEC, genomic island OI-122 effector lifA/efa1 achieved High Certainty with a large effect magnitude (OR \= 6.01, 95% CI: 2.64–13.69, P \< 0.0001), strongly supported by OI-122 type III secretion effectors nleB (OR \= 4.20, P \< 0.0001; High Certainty) and nleE (OR \= 3.80, P \= 0.0002; High Certainty).**
