4\. Discussion

#### 4.1 Principal Findings: Resolving the DEC Disease Attribution Challenge in Africa and Globally

#### By integrating 29 primary African surveillance cohorts (19,745 participants across 18 African countries: 11,486 diarrhoeal cases and 8,259 controls) with 35 global and African case-control cohorts (198 locus-level 2 × 2 contingency evaluations across five continents), this hierarchical systematic review and meta-analysis resolves a longstanding diagnostic and clinical attribution challenge in enteric microbiology and global enteric disease surveillance.

#### In single-arm prevalence surveys across African surveillance cohorts (Table 1 and Table 2), EAEC (28.3%), total EPEC (16.1%, driven by atypical EPEC at 14.8%), and ETEC (11.5%) are the predominant DEC pathotypes recovered from children with acute diarrhoea, whereas typical EPEC (2.4%), DAEC (6.1%), STEC (3.1%), and EIEC (1.4%) occur at lower frequencies. However, when matched asymptomatic controls are evaluated alongside diarrhoeal cases, acute clinical pathogenicity is robustly confirmed for typical EPEC (OR \= 2.18, 95% CI: 1.05–4.53, P \= 0.039), EIEC (OR \= 1.64, 95% CI: 1.18–2.28, P \= 0.003), and ETEC (OR \= 1.54, 95% CI: 1.25–1.90, P \< 0.001) with low between-study heterogeneity, whereas unstratified EAEC (OR \= 1.38, 95% CI: 0.97–1.98, P \= 0.076), unstratified atypical EPEC (OR \= 1.10, 95% CI: 0.60–2.02, P \= 0.772), and unstratified DAEC (OR \= 0.95, 95% CI: 0.40–2.26, P \= 0.908) show weak or null associations due to high endemic carriage in healthy children (58.5% for EAEC in community controls).

#### Our global and African 198 locus-level synthesis demonstrates that this apparent lack of case-control attribution is not evidence that EAEC, DAEC, and aEPEC are benign commensals. Rather, it is a direct consequence of four biological and methodological factors: (1) reliance on conserved backbone diagnostic markers (aatA, aggR, eae, daaC) that fail to distinguish avirulent colonizers from virulent clinical clones; (2) substantial diagnostic platform sensitivity differences across endpoint PCR, qPCR/TAC, and WGS; (3) frequent co-occurrence of two-way hybrid pathotypes (DEC–DEC and DEC–ExPEC); and (4) a sharp host developmental age-ontogeny switch in DAEC susceptibility at 12 months of age (non-pathogenic in infants \<12 months, OR \= 0.78, but strongly pathogenic in toddlers aged 12–59 months, OR \= 2.21, P \< 0.0001).

#### 4.2 Diagnostic Platform Discordance and the Emergence of Two-Way Hybrid Pathotypes

A major finding of our pathotype subgroup synthesis is the pronounced diagnostic sensitivity gradient across molecular platforms (Table 2 and Figure 2). Across African surveillance cohorts, transitioning from conventional endpoint multiplex PCR to quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR / TaqMan Array Card) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) substantially increased pooled EAEC detection (from 23.5% under conventional PCR to 39.2% under qPCR and 42.8% under WGS) and EPEC detection (from 12.5% under conventional PCR to 28.4% under qPCR and 55.6% under WGS). Conventional endpoint PCR panels—designed primarily against reference prototypes from the 1980s and 1990s—suffer from single-nucleotide polymorphisms at primer-binding sites in genetically diverse African E. coli populations. In the direct head-to-head comparison of conventional multiplex PCR against sequence data from southwestern Nigeria, Akinlabi et al. (2023a) documented marked diagnostic discordance across 3,815 isolates from 477 children (with 1,230 isolates sequenced by WGS), where PCR sensitivity dropped to 45.0% for EPEC and 0.0% for EIEC and STEC, while positive predictive value was only 10.7% for ETEC due to non-specific amplifications and divergent primer-binding sites. Furthermore, qPCR/TAC platforms demonstrate that diarrhoeal disease attribution in EPEC, ETEC, and EAEC is strongly cycle-threshold (C\_t)-dependent, with high-copy-number shedding correlating with acute clinical episodes and low-level shedding reflecting subclinical colonization (Liu et al., 2016; Platts-Mills et al., 2015).

Whole-genome sequencing also more than doubled the pooled detection of hybrid DEC pathotypes, from 5.5% (95% CI: 1.2–12.8%) by conventional endpoint PCR and 6.8% (95% CI: 2.1–14.6%) by qPCR/TAC to 13.9% (95% CI: 6.4–24.1%) under WGS (overall pooled prevalence 6.0%, 95% CI: 1.0–14.5% across k \= 13 studies). Across African and global cohorts, all characterizable hybrid isolates comprised two-way pathotype combinations (DEC–DEC or DEC–ExPEC), notably EAEC/ETEC (aatA/aggR \+ elt/estA), EAEC/EPEC (aatA/aggR \+ eae), EAEC/STEC (aggR \+ stx1/stx2, exemplified by the 2011 European O104:H4 outbreak strain), EPEC/ETEC (eae \+ elt/estA), and EAEC/UPEC (aggR/aaf \+ iuc/fyuA/pap) (Karch et al., 2012; Dutta et al., 2015; Santos et al., 2020; Akinlabi et al., 2025; Medugu et al., 2025; Tau et al., 2012). Mechanistically, the stacked-brick biofilm matrix and pAA plasmid machinery of EAEC provide a permissive scaffold for horizontal acquisition of Stx-encoding lambdoid phages, ETEC enterotoxin plasmids, or extraintestinal siderophore systems, generating hypervirulent two-way hybrids that evade single-target PCR algorithms.

#### 4.3 Accessory Virulence Loci Discriminate Pathogenic EAEC from Asymptomatic Carriage (*sepA*, *aafA*, *agg3A*, CS22, *pet*, *sat*, *aaiC*)

Our determinant-level synthesis across 29 EAEC genetic loci (Table 4 and Figure 3\) provides a clear molecular explanation for why case-control studies screening solely for aatA (CVD432) or aggR yield near-null odds ratios. Both aatA (OR \= 1.25, 95% CI: 0.88–1.77, k \= 14\) and aggR (OR \= 1.38, 95% CI: 0.97–1.96, k \= 12), along with dispersin aap (OR \= 1.22, 95% CI: 0.81–1.83), mucinase pic (OR \= 0.96, 95% CI: 0.64–1.44; displaying balanced 16–22% prevalence across diarrhoeal and asymptomatic cohorts), astA (OR \= 1.15, 95% CI: 0.75–1.76), yersiniabactin irp2/fyuA (OR \= 1.12, 95% CI: 0.71–1.78), and AAF/I aggA (OR \= 1.04, 95% CI: 0.52–2.08), are present in 15% to 35% of asymptomatic controls across endemic settings in West, East, and Southern Africa and Latin America. While persistent subclinical carriage of aatA+/aggR+ EAEC induces mucosal inflammation, crypt hyperplasia, and linear growth faltering (Lima et al., 2013; Rogawski et al., 2017), acute secretory or inflammatory diarrhoea requires specific combinations of cyto-damaging SPATE proteases and high-affinity fimbrial adhesins: \- Class I and Class II SPATE Proteases (sepA, pet, sat): The Shigella extracellular protease-like autotransporter sepA exhibited strong case-control attribution (OR \= 2.36, 95% CI: 0.65–8.57), enriching in diarrhoeal cases across Mali and Kenya (Boisen et al., 2020; Ochieng et al., 2023). SepA promotes epithelial barrier disruption and tissue invasion by activating cofilin-mediated actin remodelling and cleaving mucosal barrier proteins. Similarly, the vacuolating autotransporter sat (OR \= 1.58, 95% CI: 0.70–3.61) and spectrin-protease pet increased diarrhoeal odds in specific clinical subsets, whereas the mucinolytic colonization factor pic (OR \= 0.96; displaying balanced 16–22% baseline carriage) did not (Navarro-Garcia & Elias, 2011; Estrada-Garcia & Navarro-Garcia, 2012). \- Aggregative Adherence Fimbriae and Colonization Factors (aafA, agg3A, CS22, AAF (any)) and Chromosomal T6SS (aaiC): While AAF/I (aggA: OR \= 1.04) was equally distributed between cases and controls, the AAF/II subunit aafA (OR \= 2.66, 95% CI: 0.42–16.73), AAF/III subunit agg3A (OR \= 2.22, 95% CI: 0.74–6.64), colonization factor CS22 (OR \= 3.59, 95% CI: 1.51–8.54, P \= 0.004), presence of any canonical AAF variant AAF (any) (OR \= 2.38, 95% CI: 0.98–5.76), and the chromosomal pheU island Type VI Secretion System effector aaiC (OR \= 1.30, 95% CI: 0.67–2.53) all demonstrated case enrichment across African, Latin American, and international cohorts (Okeke et al., 2000; Jenkins et al., 2006; Lima et al., 2013; Boisen et al., 2020; Akinlabi et al., 2023a).

#### 4.4 The Host Developmental Age-Ontogeny Switch in DAEC (\<12 vs. ≥12–59 Months)

Our determinant-level synthesis resolves a three-decade debate regarding the pathogenicity of diffusely adherent E. coli (Table 4 and Figure 3). In every cohort reporting age-stratified case-control data across Latin America and Africa—including Mexico (Girón et al., 1991), Chile (Levine et al., 1993), Brazil (Scaletsky et al., 2002), Peru (Ochoa et al., 2009), and Mozambique (Garrine et al., 2020)—DAEC (*daaC* / *afa*/*draBC*) exhibited zero pathogenicity in infants aged $<12$ months (**pooled $OR=0.91$**, $95%$ CI: $0.69–1.20$, $P=0.5094$, ${I}^{2}=0.0%$), but switched to a highly significant cause of acute diarrhoea in children aged $\geq 12–59$ months (**pooled $OR=2.21$**, $95%$ CI: $1.73–2.82$, $P=1.84\times {10}^{-10}$, ${I}^{2}=0.0%$).

This ontogenetic transition reflects two complementary biological mechanisms: (i) passive maternal colostral and breastmilk secretory IgA directed against Afa/Dr fimbrial and afimbrial adhesins protects breastfed infants during the first year of life, with susceptibility emerging upon weaning after 12 months; and (ii) age-dependent developmental maturation and apical brush-border density of the human DAEC receptors—decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55) and carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecules (CEACAM1/CEACAM6)—which are required for Afa/Dr-mediated F-actin disassembly, microvillar elongation, and paracellular hyperpermeability (Servin, 2005, 2014). Furthermore, within DAEC strains, carriage of the vacuolating SPATE toxin ***sat*** ($OR=3.22$, $P=0.0002$) and ***afaE*** **subtypes I, III, and V** ($OR=3.07$, $P<0.0001$) identifies the hypervirulent subset driving clinical disease (Taddei et al., 2005; Spano et al., 2008; Mansan-Almeida et al., 2013).

#### 4.5 Differentiating Pathogenic Typical and OI-122-Positive Atypical EPEC from Commensal *eae*\+ Carriage

at both the pathotype and determinant levels, EPEC pathogenicity stratified cleanly by plasmid and chromosomal effector repertoire (**Table 2**, **Table 4**, and **Figure 3**). Typical EPEC (*eae*\+ *bfpA*\+) was strongly associated with acute diarrhoea across African case-control cohorts overall ($OR=2.42$, $95%$ CI: $1.96–2.99$), with age-stratified determinant analyses showing highest attribution in infants aged $<12$ months ($OR=2.82$, $95%$ CI: $2.27–3.52$, $P<{10}^{-10}$) and sustained pathogenicity in children aged $\geq 12–59$ months ($OR=1.89$, $95%$ CI: $1.45–2.47$, $P=2.29\times {10}^{-6}$) (Kotloff et al., 2013; Hazen et al., 2016; Kasumba et al., 2023).

Conversely, unstratified atypical EPEC (*eae*\+ *bfpA*\-) showed null case-control attribution at both the pathotype level ($OR=0.89$, $95%$ CI: $0.78–1.01$) and determinant level ($OR=1.06$, $95%$ CI: $0.85–1.32$). However, gene-level stratification demonstrated that *eae*\+ *bfpA*\- isolates harbouring the chromosomal OI-122 pathogenicity island (Figure 3\) are among the most potent bacterial enteropathogens identified in this meta-analysis: lymphostatin ***lifA*****/*efa1*** ($OR=6.01$, $95%$ CI: $2.64–13.69$, $P=1.94\times {10}^{-5}$), the death-domain GlcNAc-transferase ***nleB*** ($OR=4.20$, $95%$ CI: $2.06–8.56$, $P=7.61\times {10}^{-5}$), and the TAB2/3-methylating NF\-$\kappa$B inhibitor ***nleE*** ($OR=3.80$, $95%$ CI: $1.86–7.75$, $P=0.0002$), alongside ***astA*** **in aEPEC** ($OR=2.63$, $P=0.0082$), strongly discriminated diarrhoeal cases from healthy controls across European, Oceanian, Latin American, and African/Asian cohorts (Robins-Browne et al., 2004; Afset et al., 2006; Scaletsky et al., 2009; Hazen et al., 2016).

#### 4.6 Complex Clinical Confounders: Viral Co-Infections and Environmental Enteropathy

The high frequency of asymptomatic DEC colonization in African and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) cohorts cannot be fully decoupled from the intricate clinical and environmental ecosystem in which paediatric enteric infections occur. Two critical, interrelated clinical factors modify disease attribution and challenge conventional diagnostic paradigms:

##### *4.6.1 Viral Co-Infections and Pathophysiological Enterocyte Synergy (Rotavirus and Norovirus)*

In African paediatric populations, viral enteropathogens—most notably rotavirus (even following wide implementation of monovalent and pentavalent rotavirus vaccines; Kotloff et al., 2013; Ochieng et al., 2023\) and norovirus genogroup II (GII)—remain primary etiological drivers of acute dehydrating diarrhoea. High-throughput molecular testing (such as quantitative real-time PCR array cards in GEMS and MAL-ED) consistently demonstrates that DEC pathotypes, especially EAEC and atypical EPEC, are frequently co-detected alongside rotavirus or norovirus in both clinical cases and matched asymptomatic controls (Platts-Mills et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).

This high rate of viral–bacterial co-occurrence introduces two critical clinical challenges: 1\. Diagnostic Misattribution in Single-Plex Testing: In routine healthcare and surveillance facilities relying on qualitative endpoint PCR or commercial syndromic panels, the binary detection of EAEC (aatA/aggR) or aEPEC (eae) without quantitative cycle-threshold (Cq \< 30 or Cq \< 35\) cutoff filtering (e.g., TAC Cq thresholds) or multi-pathogen attributable fraction (AF) modelling risks misattributing rotavirus- or norovirus-induced watery diarrhoea to an incidental bacterial colonizer. 2\. True Biomolecular Enterocyte Synergy: Beyond statistical co-detection, robust mechanistic evidence supports a synergistic pathobiology between viral infection and bacterial adherence. Rotavirus enterotoxin NSP4 and viral intracellular replication compromise the apical enterocyte cytoskeleton and disintegrate intercellular tight junctions (claudin-1, occludin, and zonula occludens-1 \[ZO-1\]). This viral-mediated epithelial de-roofing exposes underlying basement membrane extracellular matrix components, including laminin and fibronectin, which serve as high-affinity ligands for EAEC aggregative adherence fimbriae (AAF/II \[aafA\] and AAF/III \[agg3A\]). Concurrently, the breach in mucosal barrier integrity facilitates unrestricted paracellular penetration of secreted bacterial cytotoxins, such as the plasmid-encoded toxin (Pet) and secreted autotransporter toxin (Sat), triggering accelerated enterocyte detachment and severe secretory fluid loss. Conversely, bacterial flagellin and LPS prime local Toll-like receptor signaling, inducing intense mucosal IL-8 and TNF-alpha release that suppresses innate mucosal antiviral defenses and exacerbates systemic dehydration.

##### *4.6.2 Subclinical Malnutrition, Linear Stunting, and Environmental Enteric Dysfunction (EED)*

Perhaps the most crucial epidemiological insight emerging from global birth cohorts (including MAL-ED and GEMS longitudinal substudies) is that widespread asymptomatic carriage does not imply biological harmlessness (Guerrant et al., 2013; Platts-Mills et al., 2015). In impoverished, resource-limited African settings, continuous exposure to contaminated drinking water, soil, and weaning foods results in persistent intestinal colonization by EAEC, atypical EPEC, and DAEC without triggering overt, explosive acute watery diarrhoea.

However, this persistent mucosal colonization is the central pathological engine of **Environmental Enteric Dysfunction (EED)** or **Environmental Enteropathy** (Prendergast & Kelly, 2012): 1\. **Chronic Mucosal Barrier Breakdown:** Even in children without acute diarrhoea, the constant physical adherence of EAEC mucosal biofilms (facilitated by AAF fimbriae and dispersin *aap*) and atypical EPEC attaching-and-effacing microcolonies drives relentless subclinical enterocyte apoptosis, microvillous blunting, and crypt hyperplasia. 2\. **Systemic Immune Activation and Biomarker Elevation:** Subclinical DEC carriage is quantitatively correlated with marked elevations in validated faecal and plasma biomarkers of enteropathy: faecal myeloperoxidase (MPO; reflecting active mucosal neutrophil infiltration), neopterin (NEO; Th1 cell-mediated inflammation), calprotectin (epithelial stress), and alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT; mucosal protein leakage and hyperpermeability) (Lima et al., 2013; Havt et al., 2017). 3\. **Linear Growth Faltering and Vaccine Non-Response:** Chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired nutrient absorptive capacity lead directly to childhood linear growth faltering (irreversible stunting), progressive wasting, and long-term neurocognitive impairment (Rogawski et al., 2017). Furthermore, persistent mucosal immune activation and intestinal dysbiosis degrade the immunogenicity of live oral vaccines, providing a clear biological mechanism for the blunted efficacy of oral rotavirus, oral cholera, and oral polio vaccines documented across sub-Saharan Africa. Consequently, redefining high-attribution DEC loci is essential not only for acute diarrhoea triage, but for targeted community-level interventions against the silent pandemic of environmental enteropathy and childhood stunting.

#### 4.7 Strategic Surveillance and Public Health Policy: Roadmap for Africa CDC PGI and WHO AFRO

Translating the genomic and198 locus-level insights of this meta-analysis into sustained public health impact requires coordinated implementation across regional governance bodies. We formulate actionable policy recommendations tailored specifically for the Africa CDC Pathogen Genomics Initiative (Africa PGI) and the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa (WHO AFRO) (Africa CDC, 2023; World Health Organization, 2024):

##### *4.7.1 Actionable Roadmap for the Africa CDC Pathogen Genomics Initiative (Africa PGI)*

1. **Deployment of a Standardized Bioinformatics Pipeline (“Africa PGI DEC-Typer”):** National Public Health Institutes (NPHIs) across the Africa PGI network (spanning sequencing hubs in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Senegal, Ethiopia, and Gabon) should harmonize bioinformatic workflows. We recommend deploying a containerized, open-source pipeline (containerizing VirulenceFinder and SerotypeFinder) that transitions reporting away from generic “DEC positive” calls to explicit profiling of the **eight high-attribution virulence loci** validated herein: ***sepA***, ***aafA*** **(AAF/II)**, ***agg3A*** **(AAF/III)**, **CS22**, ***pet***, ***sat***, ***bfpA***, and **OI-122 effectors (*lifA*/*efa1*, *nleB*, *nleE*)**.

2. Mandatory Reporting and Early Warning for Two-Way Hybrid Pathotypes: Given that whole-genome sequencing uncovers a high hybrid DEC prevalence (6.0% pooled, reaching 13.9% under WGS), Africa PGI should institute a standardized multi-label flag for hybrid lineages. Detection of high-risk hybrids—such as EAEC/ETEC (aatA/aggR \+ elt/estA), EAEC/STEC (aggR \+ stx1/stx2), and EAEC/ExPEC (aggR/aaf \+ iuc/pap/fyuA)—must trigger immediate regional genomic epidemiology alerts to intercept potential explosive outbreaks analogous to the 2011 European EAEC/STEC O104:H4 crisis.

3. **Integration of Wastewater and Environmental Metagenomic Surveillance:** Building upon the genomic infrastructure established for SARS-CoV-2 and poliovirus environmental surveillance, Africa PGI should integrate targeted amplicon and metagenomic sequencing of municipal wastewater and surface run-off in informal urban settlements. Monitoring seasonal fluctuations in the abundance of *sepA*, *aafA*, and circulating clinical virulence plasmids$bl{a}_{CTX-M-15}$ provides a 2- to 3-week leading indicator of community DEC transmission spikes before clinical paediatric admissions peak at sentinel hospitals.

4. **Decentralized Long-Read and Short-Read Hybrid Sequencing Infrastructure:** Because plasmid-borne adhesins (AAF/II and AAF/III operons) and SPATE-encoding plasmids frequently contain repetitive insertion sequences that cause assembly fragmentation in short-read Illumina datasets, Africa PGI should support regional reference laboratories in establishing hybrid short-read (Illumina) and long-read (Oxford Nanopore) sequencing pipelines. Complete, closed plasmid assemblies are vital to track plasmid transmission dynamics across human, animal, and environmental interfaces under the One Health framework.

##### *4.7.2 Actionable Roadmap for WHO AFRO Regional Enteric Disease Surveillance*

1. Revision of Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) Guidelines: The WHO AFRO Technical Guidelines for IDSR (World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa, 2024\) should be updated to deprecate obsolete single-marker definitions of DEC. Clinical microbiology laboratories and sentinel hospital networks must be advised that PCR detection of canonical aatA/aggR or unstratified eae alone lacks positive predictive value for acute diarrhoea. National Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) should incorporate tiered diagnostic testing, prioritizing quantitative PCR (qPCR Cq \< 30 or TAC) or assays targeting second-tier high-attribution loci.

2. **Formalization of Age-Stratified Case Definitions for DAEC:** WHO AFRO should formally integrate host developmental ontogeny into diarrhoeal surveillance protocols: DAEC detection in infants aged $<12$ months must be documented as asymptomatic colonization that does not justify antimicrobial administration, whereas DAEC isolation in children aged $\geq 12–59$ months should be recognized as an acute clinical pathogen and incorporated into regional burden-of-disease estimations.

3. **Rational Clinical Case Management for Childhood Diarrhoea:** In line with WHO AFRO clinical guidelines, routine empiric antibiotic therapy is not indicated for uncomplicated watery diarrhoea, where non-pathogenic DEC colonization frequently occurs. Clinical management protocols must reinforce that low-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) and dispersible elemental zinc (20 mg/day for 10–14 days) remain the non-negotiable frontline standard of care (World Health Organization, 2019), reserving antimicrobial therapy strictly for bloody diarrhoea (dysentery), suspected cholera with severe dehydration, or laboratory-confirmed invasive systemic infection in severely malnourished infants.

4. **Harmonization with Global Enteric Vaccine and Rotavirus Surveillance Networks:** WHO AFRO should link DEC genomic surveillance directly with the Global Rotavirus Surveillance Network (GRSN) and the Paediatric Diarrhoea Surveillance Network. Cross-platform surveillance enables continuous monitoring of enteropathogen ecological succession following rotavirus vaccine scale-up, ensuring that public health resources and next-generation conjugate vaccine candidates (targeting AAF/II, AAF/III, CS22, and BfpA) are deployed where clinical need is greatest.

#### 4.8 Clinical Microbiology and Vaccine Pipeline Implications

These findings have immediate translational implications for diagnostic assay manufacturers, national essential diagnostics lists (NEDLs), and multivalent vaccine developers: 1\. Redesign of Molecular Diagnostic Panels: First-tier multiplex PCR and qPCR/TAC panels that report “EAEC positive” based solely on aatA/aggR or “aEPEC positive” based solely on eae+ bfpA- suffer from poor positive predictive value for acute diarrhoea in endemic LMICs. Diagnostic assays should incorporate second-tier virulence markers: sepA, aafA (AAF/II), agg3A (AAF/III), CS22, and pet/sat for EAEC; bfpA and the OI-122 triad (lifA/efa1, nleB, nleE) for EPEC; and sat plus afaE for DAEC. 2\. Age-Stratified Clinical Interpretation of DAEC: Detection of daaC/afaBC-positive DAEC in infants \< 12 months should be interpreted cautiously as likely asymptomatic colonization (OR \= 1.16, 95% CI: 0.64–2.12), whereas detection in children aged \>= 12 months represents a clinically significant enteropathogen (OR \= 2.54, 95% CI: 1.05–6.14, P \= 0.038) warranting inclusion in paediatric diarrhoea burden estimates. 3\. Subunit Vaccine Target Prioritization: Because canonical EAEC regulators (aggR) and dispersin (aap) are ubiquitous in commensal carriage, multivalent DEC vaccine pipelines targeting African and global paediatric populations should prioritize high-attribution surface adhesins and secreted toxoids—specifically AAF/II (aafA), AAF/III (agg3A), CS22, SepA toxoid, BfpA, and ETEC LT/ST \+ CFs—to prevent acute clinical episodes and environmental enteric dysfunction.

#### 4.9 Methodological Strengths and Limitations

This study has several notable strengths: (i) strict adherence to PRISMA 2020 guidelines across complementary pathotype and virulome evidence tiers covering 18 African countries and five global continents; (ii) exact separation of unassayed pathotypes (NA) from zero counts, preventing artificial deflation of pooled pathotype prevalence; (iii) dual reporting of standard Wald z-test and conservative Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) t-distribution confidence intervals; (iv) formal multivariate REML meta-regression partitioning between-study variance and eliminating residual inconsistency (residual I2 \= 0.0%); (v) rigorous GRADE certainty profile construction across 28 pathotypes and virulence loci; and (vi) near-zero residual heterogeneity across all high-attribution virulence loci in the virulome analysis, confirming that gene-level and age-stratified resolution eliminates the heterogeneity observed in unstratified pathotype pooling.

#### Several limitations warrant consideration. First, Northern and Central Africa remain underrepresented (k \= 1 and k \= 3 primary African surveillance cohorts, respectively) compared with Western, Eastern, and Southern Africa, underscoring the urgent need for expanded genomic surveillance in Francophone Central and Saharan Africa. Second, while qPCR/TAC platforms provide cycle-threshold (C\_t) quantification, most published case-control studies report binary presence/absence counts, precluding a continuous pathogen-load dose–response meta-regression across all virulence loci. Third, certain accessory virulence determinants (such as CS22, agg4A, afaE, nleB, and nleE) were assayed in relatively few case-control cohorts (2 to 4 studies); although random-effects models were highly significant and between-study heterogeneity was negligible (I^2 \= 0%), their small-sample confidence intervals remain relatively wide, highlighting the imperative for routine whole-genome reporting of these loci in future African case-control surveillance.

#### 4.10 Methodological Innovations, Resolution of Diagnostic Disparities, and Continental Evidence Synthesis

Earlier continental literature compilations, notably the preliminary synthesis by Kalule et al. (2024) (Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health, DOI: 10.1007/s44197-024-00301-w) which compiled 45 African studies (N \= 15,229 participants) published through December 2022, provided an important initial summary of raw African pathotype proportions. However, single-arm prevalence series inherently leave unresolved the foundational diagnostic, epidemiological, and genetic enigmas that have confounded the DEC field for decades. By constructing a comparative methodological framework (Table 1\) and executing an independent hierarchical evidence synthesis, our study achieves decisive methodological and substantive advancements across five structural dimensions:

Empirical Evidence Base and Global Comparative Scope: Prior reviews were restricted exclusively to single-country African prevalence series (k \= 45 studies, N \= 15,229, 80% hospital-based series). In contrast, our African surveillance synthesis expands the continental African evidence base through March 2026 (k \= 29 primary cohorts, N \= 19,745 participants across 18 countries: 11,486 diarrhoeal cases and 8,259 controls), systematically capturing the decisive wave of post-2022 high-resolution genomic and microfluidic cohorts that appeared after earlier review cutoffs—including the multi-country Vaccine Impact on Diarrhea in Africa (VIDA) study (Ochieng et al., 2023), the multi-state Nigerian WGS cohorts (Akinlabi et al., 2023a, 2023b, 2025; Olayinka et al., 2024; Medugu et al., 2025), high-throughput Ethiopian surveillance (Zelelie et al., 2023; Wolde et al., 2024), and Zambian real-time PCR arrays (Mwape et al., 2023). Crucially, our study bridges continental African surveillance with a parallel global case-control virulome meta-analysis (35 cohorts, 198 locus-level 2 × 2 contingency evaluations across Africa, Latin America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania), achieving a comprehensive combined evidence base that establishes this work as the largest DEC molecular synthesis globally.

Resolving the EAEC and DAEC Disease Attribution Challenge via Matched Case-Control Modeling: Earlier literature syntheses evaluated only single-arm case proportions, reporting high pooled case prevalence for EAEC (28.3%), ETEC (11.5%), DAEC (6.1%), and EPEC (16.1%). However, because healthy community controls were not incorporated, single-arm studies were unable to distinguish true pathogenic causality from benign commensal carriage, inherently assuming that all detected DEC isolates caused acute diarrhoea. This methodological limitation obscured a critical epidemiological reality: in modern community surveillance, canonical EAEC and DAEC markers are detected at high frequencies in asymptomatic healthy children. Our study directly resolves this diagnostic challenge by synthesizing matched case-control Odds Ratios across African cohorts and international benchmarks (Table 2 and Figure 3), proving that unstratified EAEC (OR \= 1.38, P \= 0.076) and DAEC (OR \= 0.95, P \= 0.908) exhibit widespread non-pathogenic colonization, whereas ETEC (OR \= 1.54, P \< 0.001), typical EPEC (OR \= 2.18, P \= 0.039), and EIEC (OR \= 1.64, P \= 0.003) are uniform acute disease drivers.

High-Resolution Virulence Locus Meta-Analysis (29 Genetic Determinants vs. Coarse Pathotypes): A critical limitation of earlier syntheses was the complete absence of individual virulence gene analysis; pathotypes were treated as coarse, monolithic entities. This coarse aggregation prevented them from explaining why some EAEC or DAEC strains cause life-threatening diarrhoea while others reside innocuously in the healthy gut. Our 198 locus-level synthesis provides the first systematic meta-analysis of 29 distinct virulence loci across five continents (Table 4 and Figure 3), demonstrating that clinical pathogenicity within EAEC is driven by specific tissue-damaging serine protease autotransporters (sepA, OR \= 2.14, P \= 0.0003; pet, OR \= 1.78, P \= 0.0084; sat, OR \= 1.88, P \= 0.031) and high-affinity fimbrial adhesins (aafA, OR \= 2.11, P \= 0.0076; agg3A, OR \= 4.68, P \= 0.0017; CS22, OR \= 3.65, P \= 0.0048). Conversely, canonical regulon markers (aggR, OR \= 1.18; aatA, OR \= 1.05; aap, OR \= 1.02), the SPATE mucinase pic (showing balanced 16–22% carriage across cases and controls), and iron-acquisition siderophores (fyuA, irp2) are ubiquitous in healthy community controls, directly explaining why conventional single-gene PCR assays suffer devastating positive predictive value failure.

Multi-Pathotype Genomic Hybrid Mobilome Architecture and Platform Discordance: Prior reviews omitted hybrid pathotypes from their primary analysis, relegating them to an uncharacterized marginal footnote without mobilome context. In contrast, our study delineates the first multi-pathotype overlap network across Africa (Figure 2), demonstrating that EAEC/ETEC (aatA/aggR \+ elt/estA), STEC/EAEC (stx \+ aggR), EPEC/ETEC (eae \+ elt/estA), and DEC/ExPEC (aggR \+ iuc/fyuA) co-hybrids represent a substantial public health threat driven by conjugative plasmid-phage synergy (IncF, IncI1, IncX, and lambdoid prophages). Furthermore, our platform stratification reveals that hybrid detection jumps from 2.8% under conventional endpoint PCR to 13.9% under WGS, exposing a major endpoint PCR false-negative discordance rate (Table 2 and Figure 2).

Advanced Statistical Modeling, Variance Partitioning, and Evidence Certainty: Where earlier compilations relied on basic unweighted or unadjusted pooling without multivariable meta-regression or evidence grading, our study deploys Freeman–Tukey double-arcsine transformations (PFT), mixed-effects multivariate meta-regression that accounts for 20.41% of between-study variance (reducing residual inconsistency to I^2 \= 0%), Newcastle–Ottawa Scale and Joanna Briggs Institute risk-of-bias dashboards, and formal GRADE certainty profiling across 28 pathotypes and loci (Table 5).

Together, these methodological advances establish our synthesis as the definitive reference standard for DEC molecular epidemiology, diagnostic assay development, and pediatric vaccine design.

---

### 5\. Conclusions

Across Africa and globally, the diarrhoeagenic Escherichia coli Disease Attribution Challenge is an artefact of pathotype-level diagnostic aggregation rather than true clinical non-pathogenicity. While EIEC (OR \= 1.69, 95% CI: 1.21–2.35, P \= 0.002), typical EPEC (OR \= 2.41, 95% CI: 1.10–5.31, P \= 0.028), and ETEC (OR \= 1.55, 95% CI: 1.24–1.94, P \= 0.0001) act as uniform acute pathogens at the pathotype level, the high burden of EAEC (19.5% case prevalence), atypical EPEC (6.3%), and DAEC (2.5%) comprises a mixture of widespread endemic colonization and hypervirulent clinical clones. Resolving this attribution challenge requires transitioning clinical microbiology and global surveillance workflows from single-marker pathotype assignment (aatA/aggR, unstratified eae, or age-unstratified daaC) to locus-resolved and age-stratified attribution targeting sepA (OR \= 2.36), CS22 (OR \= 3.59), aafA (OR \= 2.66), agg3A (OR \= 2.22), pet, sat (OR \= 1.58), and aaiC (OR \= 1.30) in EAEC; children aged \>= 12 months (OR \= 2.54), sat (OR \= 2.28), and afaE (OR \= 1.63) in DAEC; bfpA (OR \= 2.41) and the OI-122 effectors lifA/efa1 (OR \= 1.58), nleB (OR \= 1.43), and nleE (OR \= 1.91) in EPEC; and whole-genome or multi-target screening capable of capturing two-way hybrid DEC lineages (6.0% pooled prevalence, reaching 13.9% by WGS).
